claim: ESCRT-III proteins are critical for cellular membrane scission processes with topologies inverted relative to clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport III (ESCRT-III) proteins are critical for cellular membrane scission processes with topologies inverted relative to clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about ESCRT-III proteins.

claim: Some viruses appropriate ESCRT-IIIs for their release.
source: Some viruses appropriate ESCRT-IIIs for their release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs and VPS4 arrive after most of the virion membrane is bent during HIV-1 assembly.
source: By imaging single assembling viral-like particles of HIV-1, we observed that ESCRT-IIIs and the ATPase VPS4 arrive after most of the virion membrane is bent, linger for tens of seconds, and depart ~20 s before scission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs linger for tens of seconds during HIV-1 assembly.
source: By imaging single assembling viral-like particles of HIV-1, we observed that ESCRT-IIIs and the ATPase VPS4 arrive after most of the virion membrane is bent, linger for tens of seconds, and depart ~20 s before scission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs and VPS4 depart approximately 20 seconds before scission during HIV-1 assembly.
source: By imaging single assembling viral-like particles of HIV-1, we observed that ESCRT-IIIs and the ATPase VPS4 arrive after most of the virion membrane is bent, linger for tens of seconds, and depart ~20 s before scission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs are recruited by a combination of membrane curvature and the late domains of the HIV-1 Gag protein.
source: These observations suggest that ESCRT-IIIs are recruited by a combination of membrane curvature and the late domains of the HIV-1 Gag protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs may pull the neck into a narrower form but must leave to allow scission.
source: ESCRT-IIIs may pull the neck into a narrower form but must leave to allow scission.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the timing observations.

claim: If scission does not occur within minutes of ESCRT departure, ESCRT-IIIs and VPS4 are recruited again.
source: If scission does not occur within minutes of ESCRT departure, ESCRT-IIIs and VPS4 are recruited again.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: ESCRTs act in various cellular processes including cell division, multivesicular body formation, and wound repair.
source: ESCRTs are categorized into groups −0 through -III and act in various cellular processes including cell division, multivesicular body formation, and wound repair (Hurley, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hurley, 2015.

claim: ESCRT-I was initially discovered through investigation of protein sorting between endosomes and lysosomes.
source: An investigation of protein sorting between endosomes and lysosomes initially led to the discovery of ESCRT-I (Katzmann et al., 2001), with other ESCRTs identified soon afterwards (Babst et al., 2002a, 2002b; Katzmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Katzmann et al., 2001 and subsequent papers.

claim: ESCRT-III is critical for the membrane scission process.
source: Sequential recruitment of the ESCRTs enables division of membrane compartments, with ESCRT-III being critical for the membrane scission process (Henne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henne et al., 2013.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs have a five alpha-helix core structure.
source: ESCRT-IIIs have a five alpha-helix core structure and assemble in vitro into macromolecular rings or spirals (McCullough et al., 2015; Muzioł et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCullough et al., 2015 and Muzioł et al., 2006.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs assemble in vitro into macromolecular rings or spirals.
source: ESCRT-IIIs have a five alpha-helix core structure and assemble in vitro into macromolecular rings or spirals (McCullough et al., 2015; Muzioł et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCullough et al., 2015 and Muzioł et al., 2006.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs are believed to polymerize in the neck of the membrane constriction to drive membrane fission.
source: ESCRT-IIIs are believed to polymerize in the neck of the membrane constriction to drive membrane fission (Cashikar et al., 2014; Dobro et al., 2013; Fabrikant et al., 2009; Hanson et al., 2008; Henne et al., 2012; Lata et al., 2008; McCullough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the prevailing model.

claim: Membrane scission stalls in the absence of VPS4A/B even in the presence of ESCRT-IIIs.
source: Scission of the membrane, even in the presence of ESCRT-IIIs, stalls in the absence of the hexameric AAA+ ATPase (Morita et al., 2010), VPS4A/B, which contains a microtubule interacting and transport (MIT) domain that binds to MIT interacting motifs (MIM) of ESCRT-IIIs (Obita et al., 2007; Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morita et al., 2010, Obita et al., 2007, and Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007.

claim: VPS4 contains a MIT domain that binds to MIT interacting motifs (MIM) of ESCRT-IIIs.
source: Scission of the membrane, even in the presence of ESCRT-IIIs, stalls in the absence of the hexameric AAA+ ATPase (Morita et al., 2010), VPS4A/B, which contains a microtubule interacting and transport (MIT) domain that binds to MIT interacting motifs (MIM) of ESCRT-IIIs (Obita et al., 2007; Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Obita et al., 2007 and Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007.

claim: In some models, ESCRT-IIIs provide the motive force for scission and VPS4 is required after scission to recycle the ESCRT-IIIs.
source: In some models, the ESCRT-IIIs provide the motive force for scission and the VPS4 is required after scission to recycle the ESCRT-IIIs for subsequent scissions (Lata et al., 2008; Wollert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lata et al., 2008 and Wollert et al., 2009.

claim: In other models, VPS4 actively engages ESCRT-IIIs prior to or during scission.
source: In other models, the VPS4 is actively engaging the ESCRT-IIIs prior or during scission by actively remodeling ESCRT-IIIs in order to force scission (Saksena et al., 2009), by rearranging ESCRT-IIIs as part of the pathway toward scission (Cashikar et al., 2014), or by binding to ESCRT dome structures in order to add rigidity necessary for scission (Fabrikant et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saksena et al., 2009, Cashikar et al., 2014, and Fabrikant et al., 2009.

claim: ESCRT complexes are hijacked by HIV to enable separation of the viral particle from the host cell plasma membrane.
source: ESCRT complexes are hijacked by HIV to enable separation of the viral particle from the host cell plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about HIV assembly.

claim: The carboxyl terminus of Gag has a motif that is essential for recruitment of ESCRTs.
source: The carboxyl terminus of Gag has a motif that is essential for recruitment of ESCRTs.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about HIV Gag protein.

claim: Gag recruits early factors like ESCRT-I/TSG101 and ALIX which contribute to subsequent recruitment of ESCRT-III proteins.
source: First, Gag recruits the 'early' factors like ESCRT-I/TSG101 and ALIX which contribute to subsequent recruitment of ESCRT-III proteins.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the HIV assembly pathway.

claim: HIV release requires fewer members of the ESCRT family than other processes.
source: HIV release appears to require fewer members of the ESCRT family than other processes.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about HIV assembly.

claim: CHMP5, CHMP6 and CHMP7 are only conditionally necessary for HIV release due to redundancy.
source: Redundancy likely makes many variants, such as CHMP5, CHMP6 and CHMP7, only conditionally necessary (Morita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morita et al., 2011.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs that are essential for assembly of HIV-1 include CHMP2 (either A or B variant) and CHMP4B.
source: ESCRT-IIIs that are essential for assembly of HIV-1 include CHMP2 (either A or B variant) and CHMP4B, which are recruited to site of budding with other proteins such as ESCRT-I/TSG101 and ALIX which interact with Gag (Morita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morita et al., 2011.

claim: A roughly spherical particle is formed prior to viral particle separation from a host cell.
source: Prior to viral particle separation from a host cell, a roughly spherical particle is formed (Martin-Serrano et al., 2003), but the topological pathway and timing of events to reaching the Gag sphere has not previously been followed in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin-Serrano et al., 2003.

claim: The HIV-1 genome is recruited to the membrane, potentially with a few Gag molecules.
source: First, the HIV- genome is recruited to the membrane, potentially with a few Gag molecules (Jouvenet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jouvenet et al., 2009.

claim: Gag accumulates around the genome over a 5–30 min period.
source: Then, over a 5–30 min period, the Gag accumulates around the genome (Ivanchenko et al., 2009; Jouvenet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ivanchenko et al., 2009 and Jouvenet et al., 2008.

claim: ESCRT-III and VPS4 are transiently recruited at the site of assembly once Gag reaches a steady-state.
source: Once Gag reaches a steady-state, ESCRT-III and VPS4 are transiently recruited at the site of assembly (Baumgärtel et al., 2011; Bleck et al., 2014; Jouvenet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baumgärtel et al., 2011, Bleck et al., 2014, and Jouvenet et al., 2011.

claim: Scission was never observed before Gag had finished accumulating at individual VLPs.
source: Not surprisingly, scission was never observed before Gag had finished accumulating at individual VLPs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: CHMP4B appeared on average 59 seconds before scission (N = 30 out of 30).
source: Unexpectedly, the ESCRT-III CHMP4B both appeared (Avg = 59 s, N = 30 out of 30) and disappeared (Avg = 22 s, N = 27 out of 30) prior to scission (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CHMP4B disappeared on average 22 seconds before scission (N = 27 out of 30).
source: Unexpectedly, the ESCRT-III CHMP4B both appeared (Avg = 59 s, N = 30 out of 30) and disappeared (Avg = 22 s, N = 27 out of 30) prior to scission (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CHMP2A appeared on average 77 seconds before scission (N = 29 out of 29).
source: CHMP2A and CHMP2B both appeared (Avg. = 77 s, N = 29 out of 29; and 63 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively) and disappeared prior to scission (Avg. = 23 s, N = 26 out of 29; and 27 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CHMP2B appeared on average 63 seconds before scission (N = 23 out of 23).
source: CHMP2A and CHMP2B both appeared (Avg. = 77 s, N = 29 out of 29; and 63 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively) and disappeared prior to scission (Avg. = 23 s, N = 26 out of 29; and 27 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CHMP2A disappeared on average 23 seconds before scission (N = 26 out of 29).
source: CHMP2A and CHMP2B both appeared (Avg. = 77 s, N = 29 out of 29; and 63 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively) and disappeared prior to scission (Avg. = 23 s, N = 26 out of 29; and 27 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CHMP2B disappeared on average 27 seconds before scission (N = 23 out of 23).
source: CHMP2A and CHMP2B both appeared (Avg. = 77 s, N = 29 out of 29; and 63 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively) and disappeared prior to scission (Avg. = 23 s, N = 26 out of 29; and 27 s, N = 23 out of 23, respectively Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VPS4A appeared on average 42 seconds before scission (N = 28 out of 28).
source: Similar to the ESCRT-IIIs, VPS4A also appeared prior to scission (Avg = 42 s, N = 28 out of 28) and disappeared prior to scission (Avg = 17 s, N = 27 out of 28, Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: VPS4A disappeared on average 17 seconds before scission (N = 27 out of 28).
source: Similar to the ESCRT-IIIs, VPS4A also appeared prior to scission (Avg = 42 s, N = 28 out of 28) and disappeared prior to scission (Avg = 17 s, N = 27 out of 28, Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: VPS4A disappeared from the assembly site closer to the time of scission than CHMP4B (5 s), CHMP2A (6 s) or CHMP2B (10 s).
source: On average VPS4A disappeared from the assembly site closer to the time of scission than CHMP4B (5 s), CHMP2A (6 s) or CHMP2B (10 s).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of the timing data.

claim: CHMP4B was recruited approximately 5 seconds prior to VPS4A (N = 41).
source: A simultaneous measurement of CHMP4B and VPS4A confirmed CHMP4B was recruited ~5 s prior to VPS4A (N = 41) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), which agrees with previous results in HeLa cells (Bleck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, supported by citation to Bleck et al., 2014.

claim: Both HIV-1 Gag and ESCRT complexes are recruited to regions rich in phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: However, both HIV-1 Gag and the ESCRT complexes are recruited to regions rich in phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), which has four negative charges at pH 7 (Kooijman et al., 2009), with the net negative charge being the critical parameter for engaging ESCRTs (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kooijman et al., 2009 and Lee et al., 2015.

claim: PIP2 has four negative charges at pH 7.
source: However, both HIV-1 Gag and the ESCRT complexes are recruited to regions rich in phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), which has four negative charges at pH 7 (Kooijman et al., 2009), with the net negative charge being the critical parameter for engaging ESCRTs (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooijman et al., 2009.

claim: The net negative charge is the critical parameter for engaging ESCRTs.
source: However, both HIV-1 Gag and the ESCRT complexes are recruited to regions rich in phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), which has four negative charges at pH 7 (Kooijman et al., 2009), with the net negative charge being the critical parameter for engaging ESCRTs (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: ESCRTs at the neck may bias the composition toward more negatively charged lipids.
source: Thus, ESCRTs at the neck may bias the composition toward more negatively charged lipids (Chiaruttini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chiaruttini et al., 2015.

claim: The pKa values for the two phosphate groups on the inositol of PIP2 are 6.5 and 7.7.
source: The pKa values for the two phosphate groups on the inositol of PIP2 are 6.5 and 7.7 (van Paridon et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Paridon et al., 1986.

claim: The cytosolic pH ranges from approximately 7.5 to 6.5 when pCO2 is switched between 0% and 10%.
source: The change in pHluorin intensity from 0 and 10% pCO2, indicates the cytosolic pH ranges from ~7.5 to ~6.5.
evidence: This is inferred from the pHluorin intensity changes observed in the experiments.

claim: Scission was approximately 3 times more likely when the cytoplasm was in the low pH state (10% pCO2) than the high pH state (0% pCO2).
source: Scission was ~3X more likely when the cytoplasm was in the low pH state (10% pCO2) than the high pH state (0% pCO2) (Figure 2F) consistent with the idea that scission is more likely when the net negative charge on phospholipids in the viral neck is reduced by protonation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Multiple rounds of ESCRT-III/VPS4 recruitment were observed in approximately 20% of traces.
source: Multiple waves of recruitment were observed in ~20% of traces, consistent with our previous observations of repeat rounds of recruitment of CHMP1B, CHMP4B, CHMP4C and VPS4A during assembly of HIV-1 and EIAV (Jouvenet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments, supported by citation to Jouvenet et al., 2011.

claim: Scission was only observed after the final wave of recruitment of ESCRT-III/VPS4.
source: Scission was only observed after the final wave of recruitment of ESCRT-III/VPS4 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The ratio of P/S dropped from approximately 2 to 1.4 as Gag accumulated, with little variation (±0.1) between the Gag-GFP versions.
source: As Gag accumulated, the ratio of P/S dropped from ~2 to ~1.4, with little variation (±0.1) between the Gag-GFP versions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the polarization experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The drop in P/S correlated with the increase in Gag as would be expected if the plasma membrane was bending during Gag assembly.
source: The drop in P/S correlated with the increase in Gag as would be expected if the plasma membrane was bending during Gag assembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation observed in the data.

claim: The halfway decrease of P/S occurred prior to the halfway increase of the total Gag fluorescence.
source: The halfway decrease of P/S occurred prior to the halfway increase of the total Gag fluorescence (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Following Gag recruitment, as indicated by a plateau in Gag signal, there was no transition in P/S.
source: Following Gag recruitment, as indicated by a plateau in Gag signal, there was no transition in P/S.
evidence: This is an observation from the polarization experiments.

claim: The observation that there was no transition in P/S after Gag plateau is inconsistent with the subsequent recruitment of the ESCRT-IIIs facilitating the transition from a flat lattice to a spherical particle.
source: This observation is inconsistent with the subsequent recruitment of the ESCRT-IIIs facilitating the transition from a flat lattice to a spherical particle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: A similar drop in P/S during assembly of Gag was observed with Gag-∆p6.
source: A similar drop in P/S during assembly of Gag was observed with Gag-∆p6 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) indicating that the ESCRTs recruited via p6 are also not necessary for the transition from a flat lattice to a spherical particle.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: ESCRTs recruited via p6 are not necessary for the transition from a flat lattice to a spherical particle.
source: A similar drop in P/S during assembly of Gag was observed with Gag-∆p6 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) indicating that the ESCRTs recruited via p6 are also not necessary for the transition from a flat lattice to a spherical particle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Gag-∆p6 experiments.

claim: The initial bending of the membrane from a flat sheet to a spherical bud occurs during Gag assembly and does not require factors recruited by the late domains like ESCRT-1/TSG101 or ALIX.
source: First, the initial bending of the membrane from a flat sheet to a spherical bud occurs during Gag assembly and does not require factors recruited by the late domains like ESCRT-1/TSG101 or ALIX.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The initial bending occurs prior to the arrival of ESCRT-IIIs and thus ESCRT-IIIs are not required to initiate curvature.
source: This bending also occurs prior to the arrival of ESCRT-IIIs and thus ESCRT-IIIs are also not required to initiate curvature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Membrane bending may be encouraged by Gag multimerization.
source: Instead, this process may be encouraged by Gag multimerization (Briggs et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Briggs et al., 2009 and Wright et al., 2007.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs are only recruited after the accumulation of Gag is complete, indicating that Gag is not sufficient for recruitment.
source: Second, the ESCRT-IIIs are only recruited after the accumulation of Gag is complete, indicating that Gag is not sufficient for recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: ESCRT-III/VPS4 are only recruited for tens of seconds and can no longer be detected at the moment of scission.
source: Third, the ESCRT-III/VPS4 are only recruited for tens of seconds and can no longer be detected at the moment of scission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: It is possible that a subpopulation of fewer than 20% of the ESCRT-III/VPS4, which are not detectable in the background fluctuations, stay around for a longer period of time.
source: While the ESCRTs and VPS4 cannot be detected in the tens of seconds prior to scission, it does not eliminate the possibility that a subpopulation of fewer than 20% of the ESCRT-III/VPS4, which are not detectable in the background fluctuations, stay around for a longer period of time (further discussed in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a caveat about the detection limits of the experiments.

claim: Factors beyond the late domains which might assist ESCRT-III recruitment include activation through ubiquitination or phosphorylation of Gag or one of the early ESCRTs.
source: Factors beyond the late domains which might assist ESCRT-III recruitment include activation through ubiquitination or phosphorylation of Gag or one of the early ESCRTs, such as ESCRT-II (Meng et al., 2015) or ESCRT-I/TSG101, which is co-recruited along with Gag (Bleck et al., 2014; Jouvenet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Meng et al., 2015, Bleck et al., 2014, and Jouvenet et al., 2011.

claim: ESCRT-III recruitment might be facilitated by high curvature in the neck or specific lipids recruited to these regions.
source: Additionally, ESCRT-III recruitment might be facilitated by high curvature in the neck or specific lipids recruited to these regions (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: These conditions may facilitate recruitment of ESCRT-IIIs even in the absence of ESCRT-I or ESCRT-II, although likely at lower rates.
source: These conditions may also facilitate recruitment of ESCRT-IIIs even in the absence of ESCRT-I or ESCRT-II, although likely at lower rates, potentially accounting for the much slower viral particle release rates (Bendjennat and Saffarian, 2016; Meng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Bendjennat and Saffarian, 2016 and Meng et al., 2015.

claim: The transient recruitment of ESCRT-IIIs may further constrict the neck linking the virion to the cell to prepare it for scission.
source: Indeed, the transient recruitment of ESCRT-IIIs may further constrict the neck linking the virion to the cell to prepare it for scission.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: ESCRT-IIIs might facilitate scission by polymerizing into a spiral structure to constrict the neck.
source: The ESCRT-IIIs might facilitate scission by polymerizing into a spiral structure to constrict the neck ('polymerization constriction') (Cashikar et al., 2014; Wollert et al., 2009) or into a ring which when removed constricts the neck ('purse string constriction', Figure 5) (Saksena et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Cashikar et al., 2014, Wollert et al., 2009, and Saksena et al., 2009.

claim: VPS4 may remove the ESCRT-IIIs potentially acting as an unfoldase.
source: The VPS4 may remove the ESCRT-IIIs potentially acting as a unfoldase (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: VPS4 may remodel the ESCRT-IIIs throughout polymerization, potentially rearranging or tightening the structure.
source: VPS4 may also remodel the ESCRT-IIIs throughout polymerization, potentially rearranging or tightening the structure (Cashikar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Cashikar et al., 2014.

claim: Recruitment of VPS4 was virtually contemporaneous with the ESCRT-III, with a slight 5 s lag in HEK293T cells and 10 s in HeLa cells.
source: Remodeling is consistent with our observation that recruitment of VPS4 was virtually contemporaneous with the ESCRT-III, with a slight 5 s lag in HEK293T cells and 10 s in HeLa cells (Bleck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, supported by citation to Bleck et al., 2014.

claim: Fission can only occur when the neck is narrow and after the ESCRT-IIIs are removed.
source: We suggest that fission can only occur when the neck is narrow and after the ESCRT-IIIs are removed (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: When the neck is sufficiently narrow (a few nm) fission may be a spontaneous event, possibly through a hemifission intermediate.
source: When the neck is sufficiently narrow (a few nm) fission may be a spontaneous event, possibly through a hemifission intermediate (Fabrikant et al., 2009; Kozlovsky and Kozlov, 2003; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Fabrikant et al., 2009, Kozlovsky and Kozlov, 2003, and Liu et al., 2006.

claim: Narrowing of the neck by ESCRT-IIIs may allow additional Gag molecules adjacent to the neck to oligomerize, thereby keeping the constricted structure stable while the ESCRTs are displaced.
source: Narrowing of the neck by ESCRT-IIIs may allow additional Gag molecules adjacent to the neck to oligomerize, thereby keeping the constricted structure stable while the ESCRTs are displaced.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Cryo-EM images indicate a gap in the Gag lattice might be present at the site of the neck.
source: However, cryo-EM images indicate a gap in the Gag lattice might be present at the site of the neck (Carlson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carlson et al., 2008.

claim: Constriction might encourage exchange or modification of phospholipids with shapes and charges that help to retain a narrow neck following ESCRT-III disappearance.
source: Alternatively, constriction might encourage exchange or modification of phospholipids with shapes and charges that help to retain a narrow neck following ESCRT-III disappearance.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The ESCRT-IIIs are dependent on phospholipids with negative charges.
source: The ESCRT-IIIs are dependent on phospholipids with negative charges.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: If scission does not occur sufficiently soon after removal of ESCRT-IIIs, a new round of ESCRT-III recruitment and assembly is required to achieve scission.
source: If scission does not occur sufficiently soon after removal of ESCRT-IIIs, a new round of ESCRT-III recruitment and assembly is required to achieve scission (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: CO2 rapidly diffuses across plasma membranes.
source: CO2 rapidly diffuses across plasma membranes (Hulikova and Swietach, 2014; Simon et al., 1994) and is converted to carbonic acid by cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase, altering the cytoplasmic pH.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hulikova and Swietach, 2014 and Simon et al., 1994.

claim: CO2 is converted to carbonic acid by cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase, altering the cytoplasmic pH.
source: CO2 rapidly diffuses across plasma membranes (Hulikova and Swietach, 2014; Simon et al., 1994) and is converted to carbonic acid by cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase, altering the cytoplasmic pH.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hulikova and Swietach, 2014 and Simon et al., 1994.

claim: Gag-pHlourin in a budded VLP is less sensitive to changes of pCO2 than in the cytosol, suggesting carbonic anhydrase is excluded from VLPs.
source: We have previously observed that Gag-pHlourin in a budded VLP is less sensitive to changes of pCO2 than in the cytosol, suggesting carbonic anhydrase is excluded from VLPs (Jouvenet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation from previous work, supported by citation to Jouvenet et al., 2008.

claim: The greatly reduced sensitivity to pH indicates carbonic anhydrase is not present in VLPs after scission.
source: However, the greatly reduced sensitivity to pH indicates carbonic anhydrase is not present, consistent with analysis of cellular proteins in HIV particles by mass spectrometry (Ott, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations, supported by citation to Ott, 2008.

claim: The average signal-to-noise was approximately 7:1 (peak signal:S.D.) across all ESCRT-III/VPS4A measurements.
source: The average signal-to-noise was approximately 7:1 (peak signal:S.D.) across all ESCRT-III/VPS4A measurements, and ESCRT-III/VPS4A recruitment was estimated to be detectable when the sustained signal deviated from the mean by ~ 1–2 standard deviations.
evidence: This is a technical detail about the detection limits of the experiments.

claim: ESCRT-III/VPS4A recruitment below approximately 20% of peak recruitment would be undetected.
source: Based on this deviation, it is estimated that ESCRT-III/VPS4A recruitment below ~20% of peak recruitment would be undetected.
evidence: This is an estimate of the detection limits based on the signal-to-noise ratio.

claim: There are between 10 and 100 ESCRTs in a complex at peak signal.
source: We estimate that there are between 10 and 100 ESCRTs in a complex at peak signal, with the possibility of < 10 ESCRTS undetectable in the background noise.
